The final answer of 6 (the octahedron) looks correct, though I did not check every cut by hand.

**Reduction.** A conflict-free cut exists exactly when some proper nonempty vertex set S has an edge boundary with no conflicting pair. This is a valid reduction, since any disconnecting set contains such a boundary and subsets of conflict-free sets stay conflict-free.

**Orientation.** The given orientation has out-degree 2 at every vertex. It uses exactly the 12 octahedron edges, which are all pairs except 16, 25 and 34. The six conflict pairs are therefore a perfect matching on the edges.

**Cuts checked.**
- **Single vertices:** the star at v contains v's own pair, so it is blocked.
- **Pairs:** for S = {1,2}, vertex 2's pair {23, 24} lies entirely in the boundary. The antipodal case S = {1,6} is blocked by vertex 1's pair {12, 14}.
- **Triples containing an antipodal pair:** for S = {1,6,2}, vertex 2 has both out-neighbours 3 and 4 outside S, so it is blocked.
- **Triangles:** a triangle cut is unblocked only if both complementary triangles are directed 3-cycles. The four complementary pairs listed each have one non-cyclic side, so all are blocked.

I did not verify every triple with an antipodal pair, but the sampled cases and the structure of the argument are consistent.

**Uniqueness.** The octahedron is the smallest simple 4-regular planar graph. I believe the published result names it as the single exception, but I am recalling that from memory and have not confirmed it against the paper.

The exceptional graph has 6 vertices.
